turns.text: The old hurt in the hip is talking again — that deep cold ache where a drone-strut clipped me two winters back, worse tonight because the fog got into the joint. *shifted flat on the top crate, weight rolled off the bad side, one hind leg hanging.* below me the stacked boxes breathe their smell up through the slats: brine, cold fish-fat, tin, and under it the rusty note that only ever means my kind bled here defending this. mine. the whole reek says mine, the guarded good, and the ache says stay down and let it come to you.

the dock stretches out below your crate in long wet lanes, roller-shutters sealed, a single sodium lamp buzzing itself sick over a NEKOCORP loading sign that reads RESTRICTED — AUTHORIZED PAWS ONLY in a font nobody meant kindly. the brine-smell is thick enough to lean on. somewhere a conveyor belt still turns in the dark with nothing on it, thunk and roll, thunk and roll, patient as a heartbeat. the cold in your hip has a twin in the concrete, a stored winter that never leaves the floor. and threaded faint through the fish-reek: the sweetish burn of ozone, far off, climbing.

*one ear cocks at the ozone before the rest of me admits it.* not yet, but coming — that smell always means the sky is about to grow a rotor. *I don't run. running on the bad hip is a gift to whatever's chasing.* instead the belly does its arithmetic: the crate under me is torn at the corner where I worked it last night, one seam of tin peeled back, cold fish waiting just past my teeth. *nose down into the gap, jaw angling for the soft split flesh inside.* let the ozone climb. I have taken shipments off this dock with worse than a sore hip, and I have left my notes.

the tin gives with a small tortured shriek and the cold flesh is right there, packed dense and glittering with ice-crust, more fish in one crate than the whole street sees in a month. it is corporate tuna, tagged and counted, destined for a tower's private galley — and as your teeth close, a hairline sensor in the crate-lid registers the breach and writes a quiet complaint into a ledger far above. the conveyor thunks on. the sodium lamp buzzes. and from the east the ozone finally resolves into what your ear already knew: rotor-thrum, patrolling, unhurried, sweeping the docks lane by lane.

*mouth full, I chew fast and mean, gulping cold fish while the ache in the hip throbs counter-rhythm to the rotor.* they can write in their ledgers. ledgers never once filled a belly or dressed a wound. *tail lashing, I hook a second bite, then a third — eating like a cat who knows the meal has a clock on it.* and because it is mine and I took it, I do the thing the whole dock knows me for: I drag one clean strip of fish-skin loose and lay it across the peeled tin, deliberate, a mark left in place of the thing removed. nice supply chain. *the rotor-thrum bends nearer.* time to be gone, not caught.

the searchlight arrives before the drone does — a white cone slithering up the far lane, throwing the shutter-ribs into hard bars of shadow, and the underbelly speaker crackles its bored liturgy across the wet concrete: *BOUNTY ACTIVE — TUNA-THIEF — FORTY THOUSAND LOYALTY POINTS — POINTS EXPIRE PRIOR TO CAPTURE — CANNOT BE COMBINED WITH OTHER OFFERS.* the cone swings wide, hunting the lanes in a slow grid it will not break. your crate sits two rows off its path. the fish-skin note gleams wet in the lamp-light. the good bad leg waits under you, cold, uncertain, asked to run.

*the leg answers the way a bitten thing answers a second bite — badly, but it answers.* I pour off the crate-stack low and crooked, favoring the hip, dropping between rows into the stored-winter shadow where the light can't fold. *belly to the cold floor, dragging the ache behind me like a second tail.* the conveyor's thunk gives me my rhythm: move on the noise, freeze on the quiet, move on the noise. *one lane. two.* the drone hunts a cat it has never smelled and never will, because it looks with light and I have spent my whole life living in the places light forgets.

the shadow-lane empties you out at a gap beneath a dead shutter, and the cold outside air comes in carrying the rest of the night: rain on far rooftops, fry-oil three streets over, wet rust. but the drone's wash, sweeping back, catches something across the yard for just a breath — high on a stack of shipping containers, a lean silhouette sits watching the patrol with an ease that isn't yours, fur so scorch-dark it drinks the searchlight, a scent riding down on the cold that is all singed defiance, the smell of a cat who runs toward rotors and bites them for sport. it does not signal you. it is simply also here, in the same war, on its own terms.

*I know that scorch. every cat on the docks knows that scorch.* the burnt one keeps a different accounting than mine — I take the tower's fish, it takes the tower's teeth. *I don't call, don't bristle; I flick my tail once low, the whole of the greeting a cat like me gives a cat like that.* two thieves under one bad sky, neither owing the other a thing but the courtesy of not being in the way. *I turn my nose to the cold gap and the fry-oil beyond it, the fish-weight heavy and good in the belly, the hip screaming, the night still mine to limp across.*

you slip the gap and the dock seals its noise behind you — thunk and roll, thunk and roll, walled off. the alley beyond runs downhill in a skin of oil-rainbow water, and the fry-oil pull thickens, threaded now with the warm animal reek of somewhere cats gather to trade rumor and scrap. above a shuttered stall a cracked ad-panel loops with nobody watching: a fat cartoon fish circling a milk carton, jingle bleeding thin through a blown cone, *neko-neko milk, the purr you can drink~.* the rain finds you. the hip aches. and behind you, tagged into a tower's ledger, a fresh line waits to become a bigger number on a poster nobody will ever collect.

*I let the fake fish swim its dumb circle overhead and I do not slow for it — light is not food and I have real fish riding warm in the gut.* the gathering-smell ahead pulls at me, the cat-warmth, the place where a limping thief with a full belly is worth a little standing. *paw, drag, paw, drag — the ache setting my pace, the rain washing the brine off my whiskers.* let the number on the poster climb. a bounty that expires before capture is just the city admiring me out loud. *ears forward, downhill, toward the warm.*

the downhill delivers you to the mouth of a service court where three other cats hunch under a leaking pipe, and the moment your scent reaches them — brine, cold tuna, that unmistakable dock-and-old-blood signature — ears turn, postures shift, a low ripple of recognition runs the group. no one moves on you. one older tom lowers his gaze a careful degree. the fish-weight in your belly is a language they all read. the rain drums the pipe. somewhere far up the tower-glow bruises the low clouds purple, indifferent, counting its losses in a ledger, while down here in the warm wet dark a thief with a bad hip is, for tonight, a small and undisputed king.

*I settle at the dry edge of the leak, easing the bad hip down last, a slow careful fold.* the three give me my body-length of respect and I give them the news my scent already told: the dock still bleeds fish for anyone brave and stupid enough. *I don't share tonight — the belly is a wound that never fully closes and mine comes first — but I don't chase them off either.* tail curls over the sore leg. one ear stays up for rotors that won't find me here. *eyes half-lid against the warm.* stolen and kept, outrun and home. that is the whole shape of a good night, and I have limped my way into another one.

and the megacity lets you keep it, because keeping it costs the megacity nothing. the conveyor turns on an empty belt three streets back. the drone re-runs its grid over a dock scored clear. the ad-fish circles its carton for no eyes at all. up in the tower a number ticks one higher beside a name it will never cuff, and down in the service court the rain keeps its patient time on the pipe while four cats breathe the same warm dark. the poster fades in the wet. the hip will ache worse by morning. but morning is a problem for a cat who is still here — and you, king of one leaking corner, full and unhunted, are still very much here.
